title: Malware Traffic Analysis: A Structured Methodology
excerpt: At Black Hat India 2026, I worked through an intensive hands-on training on Advanced Malware Traffic Analysis. Here's the core methodology I took away — from defining the goal, building a high-level timeline, filtering noise with tcpdump and Wireshark, leveraging threat intelligence, all the way to producing actionable conclusions. Whether you're an incident responder or a SOC analyst, a structured approach beats gut instinct every time.

title: Threat Hunting with Zeek NetFlow and Splunk
excerpt: Full-packet captures are expensive to store and analyze at scale. Zeek (formerly Bro) solves this by transforming raw traffic into structured logs — conn.log, dns.log, ssl.log, and more. In this writeup I walk through how to generate Zeek files from a PCAP, filter noise from conn.log, apply MITRE ATT&CK TTPs inside Splunk (T1046 network discovery, T1021.002 SMB lateral movement), and use the PCR (Producer-Consumer Ratio) to surface suspicious data flows.

title: Machine Learning for Malware Detection: Zeek Anomaly Detector and Slips
excerpt: When you have too many flows to inspect manually, machine learning can prioritize what matters. I explored two tools from the Stratosphere Laboratory: Zeek Anomaly Detector (PCA-based anomaly scoring on conn.log) and Slips (a full ML-based NIDS with P2P threat sharing). Key insight — ML doesn't replace analysis skills, it ranks what to look at first. Understanding your baseline, your features, and the tool's limits is essential before trusting any alert.

title: CVE-2021-41773 Apache Path Traversal — Attack and Traffic Forensics
excerpt: At Black Hat India, we exploited CVE-2021-41773 (Apache path traversal + RCE via mod_cgi) in a live lab, then switched sides to analyze the resulting PCAP as defenders. The attacker perspective: encoding '.' as %2e bypasses the parser, /cgi-bin/../../../../../bin/sh gives a shell. The defender perspective: look for %2e patterns in HTTP requests, filter dst port 80, count unique IPs attempting the exploit. Both angles are necessary for writing effective detection rules.
